title: In Minnesota, one wind turbine stopped producing only electricity and started making something else using nothing but wind, water, and the air around it
excerpt: Farmers in Minnesota will finally save money on imported fertilizer thanks to a wind turbine that generates green ammonia using wind, air, and water.
content_html:
A Minnesotan wind turbine shows that wind energy can produce more than just electricity.

Various global industries are racing to decarbonize their operations, but many have historically struggled to do so.

The agricultural sector is among those actively working toward clean alternatives.

The University of Minnesota’s West Central Research and Outreach Center (WCROC) uses the electricity at an on-site chemical plant.

Beyond climate targets, volatile international markets are also a primary driver of the sector’s shift.

Will a facility in Minnesota prove that agriculture can save money while going green?

How fossil fuels have been feeding the world

Global food production has relied on one chemical reaction for over a century.

This is known as the Haber-Bosch process, and it was invented in the early 1900s.

The key is to create synthetic ammonia fertilizer by combining atmospheric nitrogen with natural gas or coal.

This process is extremely heat-intensive and accounts for up to 2% of total global greenhouse gas emissions.

While it is highly unsustainable, it has doubled the Earth’s food-carrying capacity and still feeds almost 50% of the population.

Experts predict that the population will peak at 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s.

Beyond producing enough food to feed all these people, other factors also impact the world’s food security.

Synthetic fertilizer is traditionally created in chemical plants that require continuous, high-volume power. This is why producers remain reliant on fossil fuel-powered grids.

Furthermore, the process relies on complex international supply chains, which raises import costs and carbon footprints.

From an environmental goal to a critical economic buffer

U.S. agriculture accounts for roughly 10% of national greenhouse gas emissions, but these emissions are notoriously hard to lower.

However, decarbonization has become fundamental, as climate change continues to threaten food security worldwide.

The warmer temperatures have shifted atmospheric patterns.

Weather has become more extreme and more difficult to predict, resulting in major crop losses and lower yields.

For American farmers, decarbonizing fertilizer is now more than a green initiative – it is a matter of financial survival.

A significant portion of synthetic fertilizer is imported into the U.S.

This leaves farmers vulnerable to geopolitical tensions, global supply chain shocks, and volatile price increases.

Furthermore, many buyers, consumer brands, and federal export standards now demand low carbon-intensity scores.

Those who fail to lower carbon footprints risk losing access to premium markets.

West Central Research and Outreach Center is addressing these challenges by changing the way wind energy is used.

A wind turbine that can reshape American agriculture

A large-scale 1.65-MW wind turbine in Morris, Minnesota, has shown that it produces more than clean power.

The University of Minnesota’s West Central Research and Outreach Center (WCROC) uses the electricity at an on-site chemical plant.

The plant is controlled by complex systems designed by the University of Minnesota Twin Cities.

This way, the wind turbine’s fluctuating output continues to produce liquid green ammonia.

Creating more sustainable fertilizer using wind, water, and air

The wind turbine’s electricity powers the operation, offsetting fossil fuels in the manufacturing process.

Electrolyzers are located on-site. They use wind energy to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gas.

Additionally, nitrogen gas is directly harnessed from the atmosphere using an air-separation unit.

Hydrogen and nitrogen are combined under pressure, resulting in carbon-free ammonia fertilizer.

Approximately one metric ton of green ammonia is produced by the pilot plant daily.

The fertilizer is stored on-site and transferred into local farm nurse tanks.

Minnesota farmers can finally achieve resilience.

Historically, nearly $1 billion was spent annually on carbon-heavy, imported synthetic fertilizer.

Using a wind turbine to create zero-carbon fertilizer locally protects farmers, national food security, and the climate.

The Morris plant proves that decarbonizing the agricultural sector is no longer a pipe dream. American farmers can regain economic control while securing national food supply more sustainably.

content_html_zh:
明尼苏达州的风力涡轮机表明，风能不仅仅可以产生电力。

全球各个行业都在竞相实现运营脱碳，但许多行业历来都在努力做到这一点。

农业部门是积极致力于清洁替代品的部门之一。

明尼苏达大学中西研究与推广中心 (WCROC) 使用现场化工厂的电力。

除了气候目标之外，动荡的国际市场也是该行业转变的主要驱动力。

明尼苏达州的一个设施能否证明农业可以在实现绿色环保的同时节省资金？

化石燃料如何养活世界

一个多世纪以来，全球粮食生产一直依赖于一种化学反应。

这被称为 Haber-Bosch 工艺，发明于 1900 年代初。

关键是通过将大气中的氮与天然气或煤炭结合来制造合成氨肥料。

这一过程的热量极其密集，占全球温室气体排放总量的 2%。

虽然它非常不可持续，但它使地球的粮食承载能力增加了一倍，并且仍然养活了近 50% 的人口。

专家预测，到2080年代中期，人口将达到峰值103亿。

除了生产足够的粮食来养活所有这些人之外，其他因素也会影响世界粮食安全。

合成肥料传统上是在需要持续大容量电力的化工厂中生产的。 这就是生产商仍然依赖化石燃料供电的电网的原因。

此外，该过程依赖于复杂的国际供应链，这增加了进口成本和碳足迹。

从环境目标到关键的经济缓冲

美国农业排放量约占全国温室气体排放量的 10%，但众所周知，这些排放量很难降低。

然而，随着气候变化继续威胁全球粮食安全，脱碳已成为根本。

气温升高改变了大气模式。

天气变得更加极端和难以预测，导致农作物严重损失和产量下降。

对于美国农民来说，脱碳化肥现在不仅仅是一项绿色倡议，更是关乎经济生存的问题。

很大一部分合成肥料是进口到美国的。

这使得农民容易受到地缘政治紧张局势、全球供应链冲击和价格波动波动的影响。

此外，许多买家、消费品牌和联邦出口标准现在要求低碳强度分数。

那些未能降低碳足迹的企业可能会失去进入高端市场的机会。

西部中央研究和推广中心正在通过改变风能的使用方式来应对这些挑战。

可以重塑美国农业的风力涡轮机

明尼苏达州莫里斯的一台大型 1.65 兆瓦风力涡轮机已证明其产生的不仅仅是清洁电力。

明尼苏达大学中西研究与推广中心 (WCROC) 使用现场化工厂的电力。

该工厂由明尼苏达大学双城分校设计的复杂系统控制。

这样，风力涡轮机的波动输出持续产生液态绿氨。

利用风、水和空气创造更可持续的肥料

风力涡轮机的电力为运行提供动力，抵消了制造过程中的化石燃料。

电解槽位于现场。 他们利用风能将水分解成氢气和氧气。

此外，使用空气分离装置直接从大气中提取氮气。

氢和氮在压力下结合，产生无碳氨肥。

试点工厂每天生产约一吨绿色氨。

肥料就地储存并转移到当地农场护士池中。

明尼苏达州的农民终于可以实现恢复力。

从历史上看，每年有近 10 亿美元用于高碳进口合成肥料。

使用风力涡轮机在当地生产零碳肥料可以保护农民、国家粮食安全和气候。

莫里斯工厂证明，农业部门脱碳不再是一个白日梦。 美国农民可以重新获得经济控制权，同时更可持续地确保国家粮食供应。
